title: Tutorials
text:
Each tutorial takes 30 minutes or less. If you are new to census data, start with Census 101. Then pick the R track or the Python track. Both tracks cover the same ground, so you only need one.
Before you begin either coding track, request a free Census API key. It arrives by email within a few minutes.
Much of this material draws on Kyle Walker’s free online book, Analyzing US Census Data: Methods, Maps, and Models in R. It is an excellent next step whichever language you use.










Tutorial



Description








Census 101: How Census Data Is Organized


Start here. Learn the difference between the decennial census and the ACS, how census geographies nest inside each other, and how to download a table from data.census.gov.






Census Data in R, Part 1: Getting Tables with tidycensus


Use the tidycensus package to pull ACS and 2020 decennial census data for North Carolina counties and Mecklenburg County census tracts.






Census Data in R, Part 2: Mapping with tidycensus and sf


Add geometry to your tidycensus requests and map census variables for North Carolina counties and Mecklenburg County census tracts.






Census Data in Python, Part 1: The Census API with requests and Polars


Call the Census API directly with requests, load the results into Polars, and build a reusable function for pulling ACS and decennial data.






Census Data in Python, Part 2: Mapping with pygris and GeoPandas


Download census boundaries with pygris, join them to your Census API results, and map North Carolina counties and Mecklenburg County census tracts with GeoPandas.

title: Census Data in R, Part 1: Getting Tables with tidycensus
text:
NoteAbout this tutorial



Time: about 25 minutes. Prerequisites: R and RStudio (or Positron) installed, basic familiarity with the tidyverse, and a Census API key. If you haven’t read Census 101 yet, skim it first.
By the end, you will be able to:

store your Census API key so that R can find it
pull ACS estimates for every county in North Carolina
pull ACS estimates for census tracts in one or more counties
find the variable IDs you need
compute percentages and their margins of error
pull 2020 decennial census counts

title: Census Data in R, Part 1: Getting Tables with tidycensus
text:
Setup
tidycensus is an R package written by Kyle Walker. It talks to the Census API for you and returns tidy data frames. Install it along with the tidyverse if you don’t have them yet:

install.packages(c("tidycensus", "tidyverse"))

Then load both packages:

library(tidycensus)
library(tidyverse)


Store your API key
Run the line below once, using the key from your email in place of the placeholder. The install = TRUE argument saves the key to a file named .Renviron in your home folder. R reads that file each time it starts, so you never have to paste the key into a script again.

census_api_key("YOUR_KEY_GOES_HERE", install = TRUE)

Restart R after you run it. You can confirm that R found the key with this line:

Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY")







WarningKeep the key out of your scripts



After you have run census_api_key() once, delete that line from your script. That way you won’t push your key to GitHub by accident.

title: Census Data in R, Part 1: Getting Tables with tidycensus
section: Your first request: income by county
text:
Your first request: income by county
get_acs() pulls data from the American Community Survey. Let’s get median household income (variable B19013_001) for every county in North Carolina:

nc_income <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  state = "NC",
  variables = "B19013_001",
  year = 2024
)

Getting data from the 2020-2024 5-year ACS

nc_income

# A tibble: 100 × 5
   GEOID NAME                             variable   estimate   moe
   <chr> <chr>                            <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>

 2 37003 Alexander County, North Carolina B19013_001    65354  4962
 3 37005 Alleghany County, North Carolina B19013_001    47172  4894
 4 37007 Anson County, North Carolina     B19013_001    47302  5753

 7 37013 Beaufort County, North Carolina  B19013_001    58357  3205

 9 37017 Bladen County, North Carolina    B19013_001    42422  6049
10 37019 Brunswick County, North Carolina B19013_001    77024  2734
# ℹ 90 more rows


You should get a tibble with 100 rows, one per county, and five columns:







Column
What it holds




GEOID
The county’s FIPS code, such as 37119 for Mecklenburg


NAME
A readable name, such as “Mecklenburg County, North Carolina”


variable
The variable ID you requested


estimate
The ACS estimate


moe
The margin of error, at a 90 percent confidence level



A few defaults are worth knowing about:

get_acs() uses the 5-year ACS unless you set survey = "acs1". With year = 2024, you get the 2020 to 2024 estimates.
Always set year yourself. The default changes as new data comes out. Setting it explicitly keeps your results reproducible.
You can write states and counties as names ("North Carolina"), abbreviations ("NC"), or FIPS codes ("37").

Now use regular dplyr to explore:

nc_income |>
  arrange(desc(estimate)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

title: Census Data in R, Part 1: Getting Tables with tidycensus
section: Naming variables and requesting several at once
text:
Naming variables and requesting several at once
Variable IDs are hard to remember. You can give them names inside c(). You can also request several variables in one call:

nc_profile <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  state = "NC",
  variables = c(
    median_income = "B19013_001",
    median_age = "B01002_001",
    total_pop = "B01003_001"
  ),
  year = 2024
)

Getting data from the 2020-2024 5-year ACS


This result is in long format. Each county appears three times, once per variable. Long data works well with ggplot2 and group_by(). If you’d rather have one row per county, ask for wide output:

nc_profile_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  state = "NC",
  variables = c(
    median_income = "B19013_001",
    median_age = "B01002_001",
    total_pop = "B01003_001"
  ),
  output = "wide",
  year = 2024
)

Getting data from the 2020-2024 5-year ACS

names(nc_profile_wide)

[1] "GEOID"          "NAME"           "median_incomeE" "median_incomeM"
[5] "median_ageE"    "median_ageM"    "total_popE"     "total_popM"    


In wide output, tidycensus adds an E suffix to estimates and an M suffix to margins of error. You get columns such as median_incomeE and median_incomeM.

title: Census Data in R, Part 1: Getting Tables with tidycensus
text:
Finding variables
The 5-year ACS has more than 25,000 variables. load_variables() downloads the full list so you can search it:

acs_vars <- load_variables(2024, "acs5")

In RStudio, run View(acs_vars) and type in the search box to filter. You can also search with code. The label column describes what each variable measures. The concept column names the table it belongs to.

acs_vars |>
  filter(str_detect(concept, regex("median household income", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  select(name, label, concept) |>
  head(12)

# A tibble: 12 × 3
   name        label                                                     concept
   <chr>       <chr>                                                     <chr>  
 1 B19013A_001 Estimate!!Median household income in the past 12 months … Median…
 2 B19013B_001 Estimate!!Median household income in the past 12 months … Median…
 3 B19013C_001 Estimate!!Median household income in the past 12 months … Median…
 4 B19013D_001 Estimate!!Median household income in the past 12 months … Median…
 5 B19013E_001 Estimate!!Median household income in the past 12 months … Median…
 6 B19013F_001 Estimate!!Median household income in the past 12 months … Median…
 7 B19013G_001 Estimate!!Median household income in the past 12 months … Median…
 8 B19013H_001 Estimate!!Median household income in the past 12 months … Median…
 9 B19013I_001 Estimate!!Median household income in the past 12 months … Median…
10 B19013_001  Estimate!!Median household income in the past 12 months … Median…
11 B19019_001  Estimate!!Total:                                          Median…
12 B19019_002  Estimate!!Total:!!1-person households                     Median…


Look closely at the results. You will see B19013_001 along with B19013A_001 through B19013I_001. The lettered versions repeat the table for specific racial and ethnic groups. For example, B19013B covers households headed by someone who is Black alone. Tables with PR in the ID cover Puerto Rico only.






TipReading labels



Labels use !! to separate levels of a table. For example, Estimate!!Total:!!Income in the past 12 months below poverty level: means “of the total, the number with income below the poverty level.” The first row of most tables (the variable ending in _001) is the total for that table. You will often use it as a denominator.

title: Census Data in R, Part 1: Getting Tables with tidycensus
text:
Computing percentages
Counts are hard to compare across counties of very different sizes. Mecklenburg has more than a million people. Tyrrell County has about 3,000. Percentages make fairer comparisons.
Table B17001 counts people by poverty status. B17001_002 is the number of people below the poverty level. B17001_001 is the number of people for whom poverty status is determined. The summary_var argument fetches the denominator alongside your variable:

nc_poverty <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  state = "NC",
  variables = c(below_poverty = "B17001_002"),
  summary_var = "B17001_001",
  year = 2024
) |>
  mutate(
    pct_poverty = 100 * estimate / summary_est,
    pct_poverty_moe = 100 * moe_prop(estimate, summary_est, moe, summary_moe)
  )

Getting data from the 2020-2024 5-year ACS

nc_poverty |>
  select(NAME, pct_poverty, pct_poverty_moe) |>
  arrange(desc(pct_poverty))

# A tibble: 100 × 3
   NAME                              pct_poverty pct_poverty_moe
   <chr>                                   <dbl>           <dbl>

 2 Scotland County, North Carolina          25.8            2.06
 3 Watauga County, North Carolina           25.5            2.09
 4 Richmond County, North Carolina          25.2            3.65
 5 Washington County, North Carolina        24.1            4.71

The summary_var values arrive in the summary_est and summary_moe columns. moe_prop() is a tidycensus helper that computes the margin of error for a proportion. When you derive a new number from ACS estimates, you should derive a new MOE for it too.

text:
Going smaller: census tracts
To look inside a county, switch geography to "tract". Tract requests need a state. They usually include one or more counties as well.

meck_income <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "NC",
  county = "Mecklenburg",
  variables = c(median_income = "B19013_001"),
  year = 2024
)

lkn_income <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",

  county = c("Mecklenburg", "Iredell", "Cabarrus"),

Watch the margins of error
Tract estimates rest on small samples, so their MOEs are much larger than county MOEs. A quick way to spot shaky estimates is to compare each MOE to its estimate:

meck_income |>
  mutate(moe_ratio = moe / estimate) |>
  arrange(desc(moe_ratio)) |>
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_ratio) |>

A tract whose MOE is 30 or 40 percent of its estimate deserves a caution note in your presentation. You may also notice some NA estimates. In Mecklenburg, they belong to tracts 9801, 9802, and 9803. Tracts numbered in the 9800s are special land-use tracts that cover places like airports and large parks. Few or no people live in them, so the Bureau can’t compute an income.






TipTop-coded values



Sort meck_income by estimate from highest to lowest and look at the top tract. Its estimate is exactly 250001, and its MOE is NA. That isn’t a real income. The ACS top-codes medians, so 250001 means “$250,000 or more.” Keep this in mind if you average incomes or rank the wealthiest tracts.

title: Census Data in R, Part 1: Getting Tables with tidycensus
text:
The 2020 decennial census
get_decennial() works much like get_acs(). There are two differences. You need to name a summary file with sumfile, and the results come back in a column called value because decennial data has no margin of error.
Total population by county from the Demographic and Housing Characteristics file:

nc_pop_2020 <- get_decennial(
  geography = "county",
  state = "NC",
  variables = c(total_pop = "P1_001N"),
  year = 2020,
  sumfile = "dhc"
)

Getting data from the 2020 decennial Census


Using the Demographic and Housing Characteristics File


Note: 2020 decennial Census data use differential privacy, a technique that
introduces errors into data to preserve respondent confidentiality.
ℹ Small counts should be interpreted with caution.
ℹ See https://www.census.gov/library/fact-sheets/2021/protecting-the-confidentiality-of-the-2020-census-redistricting-data.html for additional guidance.
This message is displayed once per session.


The Redistricting file (sumfile = "pl") has race and ethnicity counts at every level of geography. Here is the share of each Mecklenburg tract’s population that identifies as Black alone:

meck_black <- get_decennial(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "NC",
  county = "Mecklenburg",
  variables = c(black_alone = "P1_004N"),
  summary_var = "P1_001N",
  year = 2020,
  sumfile = "pl"
) |>
  mutate(pct_black = 100 * value / summary_value)

Getting data from the 2020 decennial Census


Using the PL 94-171 Redistricting Data Summary File


You can browse decennial variables the same way as ACS variables, with load_variables(2020, "pl") or load_variables(2020, "dhc").






TipWhich one should I use?



Use the decennial census for population counts and basic demographics in 2020. Use the ACS for anything about income, poverty, education, employment, or housing costs. Use it too when you need something more recent than 2020.

title: Census Data in R, Part 1: Getting Tables with tidycensus
text:
Saving your data
Save your results as a CSV so your teammates can use them:

write_csv(nc_poverty, "nc_poverty_2024.csv")

When you read the file back, tell readr that GEOID is text. Otherwise it may guess that the column is a number and drop leading zeros:

nc_poverty <- read_csv(
  "nc_poverty_2024.csv",
  col_types = cols(GEOID = col_character())
)

title: Census Data in R, Part 1: Getting Tables with tidycensus
text:
Try it yourself

Find the variable for the median gross rent (hint: search the concept column for “median gross rent”). Pull it for every North Carolina county. Which five counties have the highest rent?
Use summary_var to compute the percentage of households in each Mecklenburg tract that have no vehicle available. Table B08201 is a good place to start. Which tracts have the largest MOEs?
Compare total population in 2020 (decennial) with the 2024 ACS 5-year estimate of total population for each county. Which counties seem to be growing fastest? Why should you be cautious about this comparison?

title: Census Data in Python, Part 1: The Census API with requests and Polars
text:
NoteAbout this tutorial



Time: about 30 minutes. Prerequisites: Python 3.10 or newer, basic familiarity with data frames, and a Census API key. If you haven’t read Census 101 yet, skim it first.
By the end, you will be able to:

store your Census API key safely
read and build a Census API request URL
load API results into a Polars DataFrame and clean them
write a reusable function for pulling census data
pull ACS data for counties and census tracts, and 2020 decennial data
find the variable IDs you need

title: Census Data in Python, Part 1: The Census API with requests and Polars
section: Why talk to the API directly?
text:
Why talk to the API directly?
R users have tidycensus, which hides the Census API behind friendly functions. Python has no package that plays the same role quite as smoothly. The good news is that the API itself is simple. A request is just a URL, and the response is just a table in JSON format. Once you understand the pieces, a short function gives you most of what tidycensus offers.
This tutorial uses three libraries:

requests sends the request to the API
Polars holds and cleans the results
python-dotenv loads your API key from a file

pip install requests polars python-dotenv

title: Census Data in Python, Part 1: The Census API with requests and Polars
text:
Store your API key
Create a file named .env in your project folder. Put one line in it, using your own key:
CENSUS_API_KEY=your_key_goes_here
Then load it at the top of your script or notebook:

import os

import polars as pl
import requests
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()
API_KEY = os.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY")

load_dotenv() looks for .env in the folder that holds your script and then in each folder above it. If API_KEY comes back as None, move .env into the same folder as your script or notebook.






WarningKeep .env out of Git



Add .env to your project’s .gitignore file before you commit anything. Your key should never appear on GitHub.

title: Census Data in Python, Part 1: The Census API with requests and Polars
text:
Anatomy of a request
Every Census API request is a URL. Here is one that asks for median household income in every North Carolina county:
https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5?get=NAME,B19013_001E,B19013_001M&for=county:*&in=state:37&key=YOUR_KEY
It has five parts:








Part
Example
Meaning




Year
2024
The data vintage. For the 5-year ACS, 2024 means 2020 to 2024.


Dataset
acs/acs5
The ACS 5-year detailed tables. Others include acs/acs1, acs/acs5/subject, and dec/dhc.


get
NAME,B19013_001E,B19013_001M
The variables you want, separated by commas


for
county:*
The geography level you want. * means “all of them.”


in
state:37
A parent geography that limits the results. 37 is North Carolina’s FIPS code.



Try it. Paste the URL into your browser with your key in place of YOUR_KEY. You will see rows of text in square brackets. That is the raw JSON response.






ImportantThe API needs FIPS codes



tidycensus accepts names like "Mecklenburg". The raw API doesn’t. You must use numeric FIPS codes such as 37 for North Carolina and 119 for Mecklenburg County. You will learn how to look them up later in this tutorial.

title: Census Data in Python, Part 1: The Census API with requests and Polars
text:
Making the request in Python
Rather than building the URL by hand, give requests a dictionary of parameters. It assembles the URL and handles any special characters for you:

url = "https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5"
params = {
    "get": "NAME,B19013_001E,B19013_001M",
    "for": "county:*",
    "in": "state:37",
    "key": API_KEY,
}

response = requests.get(url, params=params)
response.status_code

200


A status code of 200 usually means success. Now look at the data:

rows = response.json()
rows[:3]

[['NAME', 'B19013_001E', 'B19013_001M', 'state', 'county'],
 ['Alamance County, North Carolina', '65651', '1854', '37', '001'],
 ['Alexander County, North Carolina', '65354', '4962', '37', '003']]


The response is a list of lists. The first inner list is the header row. Every list after that is one county.






TipWhen the key is wrong



If your key is missing or invalid, the API still returns status 200. It sends back an HTML error page instead of data, and response.json() fails with a confusing JSONDecodeError. When you see that error, check response.url. If it ends in missing_key.html or invalid_key.html, the problem is your key. Remember that you have to activate a new key through the link in your email.

Watch for missing value codes
The API doesn’t send blanks for missing values. It sends large negative numbers such as -666666666. Each code has a specific meaning, such as “too few sample cases to compute an estimate.” None of them are real values, and they will wreck an average or a color scale if you leave them in. Estimates and MOEs are never negative, so it is safe to turn every negative value into a null:

nc_income = nc_income.with_columns(
    pl.when(pl.col(c) < 0).then(None).otherwise(pl.col(c)).alias(c)
    for c in ["median_income", "median_income_moe"]
)

You rarely see these codes at the county level. They are common at the tract level.

title: Census Data in Python, Part 1: The Census API with requests and Polars
text:
A reusable function
You don’t want to repeat all of those steps for every request. The function below wraps them up. It takes a dictionary that maps readable names to variable IDs. It returns a clean DataFrame with a GEOID column.

def get_census(dataset, year, variables, geo_for, geo_in=None):
    """Request data from the Census API and return a clean Polars DataFrame.

    variables maps new column names to Census variable IDs, for example
    {"median_income": "B19013_001E"}.
    """
    url = f"https://api.census.gov/data/{year}/{dataset}"
    params = {
        "get": ",".join(["NAME", *variables.values()]),
        "for": geo_for,
        "key": API_KEY,
    }
    if geo_in is not None:
        params["in"] = geo_in

    response = requests.get(url, params=params)
    if response.status_code != 200:
        raise ValueError(f"Census API error: {response.text}")
    if response.url.endswith("_key.html"):
        raise ValueError(f"Problem with your API key. See {response.url}")

    rows = response.json()
    df = pl.DataFrame(rows[1:], schema=rows[0], orient="row")

    # Geography columns (state, county, tract, ...) come after the variables
    geo_cols = df.columns[len(variables) + 1:]
    new_names = list(variables.keys())

    return (
        df
        .rename(dict(zip(variables.values(), new_names)))
        .with_columns(
            pl.col(new_names).cast(pl.Float64),
            pl.concat_str(geo_cols).alias("GEOID"),
        )
        .with_columns(
            pl.when(pl.col(c) < 0).then(None).otherwise(pl.col(c)).alias(c)
            for c in new_names
        )
        .select("GEOID", "NAME", *new_names)
    )

Now the request from earlier takes only a few lines:

nc_income = get_census(
    dataset="acs/acs5",
    year=2024,
    variables={
        "median_income": "B19013_001E",
        "median_income_moe": "B19013_001M",
    },
    geo_for="county:*",
    geo_in="state:37",
)







TipSave the function for later



Copy get_census(), together with the import and API key lines above it, into a file named census_helpers.py in your project folder. Part 2 imports it with from census_helpers import get_census.

nc_profile = get_census(

    year=2024,

text:
Computing percentages and their MOEs
Table B17001 counts people by poverty status. B17001_002E is the number of people below the poverty level. B17001_001E is the number of people for whom poverty status is determined. Divide one by the other to get a rate:

nc_poverty = get_census(
    dataset="acs/acs5",
    year=2024,
    variables={
        "below_poverty": "B17001_002E",
        "below_poverty_moe": "B17001_002M",
        "universe": "B17001_001E",
        "universe_moe": "B17001_001M",
    },
    geo_for="county:*",
    geo_in="state:37",
)

A derived number needs a derived margin of error. The Census Bureau publishes a formula for the MOE of a proportion. The code below follows it. It uses a fallback formula when the value under the square root would be negative. This is the same calculation that tidycensus performs with moe_prop().

p = pl.col("below_poverty") / pl.col("universe")
under_root = pl.col("below_poverty_moe") ** 2 - p**2 * pl.col("universe_moe") ** 2
fallback = pl.col("below_poverty_moe") ** 2 + p**2 * pl.col("universe_moe") ** 2

nc_poverty = nc_poverty.with_columns(
    (100 * p).alias("pct_poverty"),
    (
        100
        * pl.when(under_root < 0).then(fallback).otherwise(under_root).sqrt()
        / pl.col("universe")
    ).alias("pct_poverty_moe"),
)

nc_poverty.select("NAME", "pct_poverty", "pct_poverty_moe").sort(
    "pct_poverty", descending=True
)

The 2020 decennial census
The decennial census uses the same function with a different dataset name. Decennial variable IDs end in N because they are counts, and they have no MOEs.
Total population by county, from the Demographic and Housing Characteristics file:

    dataset="dec/dhc",
    year=2020,
    variables={"total_pop": "P1_001N"},
    geo_for="county:*",
    geo_in="state:37",
)

The Redistricting file (dec/pl) has race and ethnicity counts. Here is the share of each Mecklenburg tract’s population that identifies as Black alone:

meck_black = get_census(
    dataset="dec/pl",
    year=2020,
    variables={"black_alone": "P1_004N", "total_pop": "P1_001N"},
    geo_for="tract:*",
    geo_in="state:37 county:119",
).with_columns(
    (100 * pl.col("black_alone") / pl.col("total_pop")).alias("pct_black")
)

title: Census 101: How Census Data Is Organized
text:
NoteAbout this tutorial



Time: about 20 minutes. Prerequisites: none. You don’t need to write any code for this one.
By the end, you will be able to:

explain how the decennial census differs from the American Community Survey (ACS)
read an ACS estimate together with its margin of error
describe the census geographic hierarchy and decode a GEOID
find and download a census table from data.census.gov

title: Census 101: How Census Data Is Organized
text:
Why start here?
The R and Python tutorials that follow will pull census data with a few lines of code. That code is easy to write. The hard part is knowing what to ask for. You need to pick a data product, a year, a table, and a level of geography, and each choice changes what the numbers mean. This tutorial covers the vocabulary you need to make those choices well.
Most of the material here is covered in more depth in Chapter 1 of Kyle Walker’s free online book, Analyzing US Census Data.

title: Census 101: How Census Data Is Organized
section: Two data products you will use most
text:
Two data products you will use most
The Census Bureau publishes dozens of datasets. For most Data Wrangle projects, you will use one of these two.

The decennial census
The US Constitution requires a count of every person living in the country every ten years. The most recent count took place in 2020. The decennial census asks only a few questions, such as age, sex, race, Hispanic origin, household relationship, and whether a home is owned or rented.
Because it tries to count everyone, the decennial census reports counts rather than estimates. It is published down to the census block, the smallest unit of census geography. The 2020 results are released in several files. The two you are most likely to see are:

the PL 94-171 Redistricting Data, which has basic population and race counts
the Demographic and Housing Characteristics File (DHC), which has more detail on age, sex, households, and housing







TipCounts are not perfectly exact



The Census Bureau adds a small amount of statistical noise to 2020 results through a method called differential privacy. The noise protects the confidentiality of respondents. It matters little for counties but can matter for very small areas such as individual blocks.




The American Community Survey (ACS)
The ACS is a survey sent to about 3.5 million addresses every year. It asks far more questions than the decennial census, including questions on income, poverty, education, commuting, health insurance, internet access, and housing costs. If your question involves money, work, or schooling, you probably want the ACS.
Because the ACS is a sample, it reports estimates. Each estimate comes with a margin of error (MOE). The Bureau releases two main versions:









ACS 1-year
ACS 5-year




Data collected over
12 months
60 months


Geographies covered
Areas with 65,000 or more people
All areas, down to block groups


Strength
Most current
Most reliable, and covers small areas


Latest release (as of Fall 2026)
2024
2020 to 2024



A 5-year estimate describes the whole five-year period. It is not a value for the final year. For example, the “2024 ACS 5-year” median household income for a county summarizes responses collected from 2020 through 2024.






WarningTwo rules of thumb for the ACS




Census tracts and block groups exist only in the 5-year data. They are too small for the 1-year survey.
Don’t compare overlapping 5-year periods. Comparing 2019 to 2023 with 2020 to 2024 is misleading because four of the five years are the same. Compare periods that don’t overlap, such as 2015 to 2019 with 2020 to 2024.





Reading a margin of error
Suppose the ACS reports that a census tract has a median household income of $62,000 with an MOE of $9,000. ACS margins of error use a 90 percent confidence level. So the Bureau is 90 percent confident that the true value falls between $53,000 and $71,000.
This matters when you compare places. Say a neighboring tract has an estimate of $66,000 ± $10,000. The two ranges overlap a lot, so you cannot claim that one tract really earns more than the other. Small geographies have small samples. That means large MOEs, so keep an eye on them whenever you work at the tract level.

title: Census 101: How Census Data Is Organized
text:
The geographic hierarchy
Census data is always reported for a place. The Bureau organizes places into a hierarchy. The core of it is sometimes called the “spine,” because each level nests cleanly inside the one above it.
Nation
└── Region (4)
    └── Division (9)
        └── State (50, plus DC and Puerto Rico)
            └── County (NC has 100)
                └── Census tract (about 1,200 to 8,000 people)
                    └── Block group (about 600 to 3,000 people)
                        └── Block (smallest; decennial census only)
A few things to know about the spine:

Counties are the workhorse geography for statewide comparisons. North Carolina’s 100 counties make for a manageable map.
Census tracts are drawn to hold about 4,000 people. They are the most common way to look inside a county. North Carolina has about 2,670 tracts, and Mecklenburg County has 305 of them.
Tract boundaries are redrawn every ten years. Tracts from the 2010s don’t always match tracts from the 2020s. Be careful when you compare tract data from before and after 2020.


Geographies that don’t nest
Some geographies you will care about sit off the spine. They don’t fit neatly inside counties or tracts:

Places are cities, towns, and unincorporated communities, such as Davidson, Charlotte, or Cornelius. Place boundaries can cross county lines. The town of Cary, for example, lies partly in Wake County and partly in Chatham County.
ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs) approximate ZIP codes. The Postal Service designs ZIP codes to deliver mail, not to describe communities, so ZCTAs cross county and even state lines.
Congressional districts, state legislative districts, and school districts follow political boundaries.
Metropolitan and micropolitan statistical areas group counties into regional economies. Davidson sits in the Charlotte-Concord-Gastonia metro area, which crosses into South Carolina.

When you choose a geography, pick one that matches your question. If you are asking about school funding, school districts may fit better than counties.

title: Census 101: How Census Data Is Organized
section: GEOIDs: the key that ties everything together
text:
GEOIDs: the key that ties everything together
Every census geography has a numeric identifier called a GEOID. It is built by stacking FIPS codes from each level of the spine:



Level
Digits
Example
Meaning




State
2
37

So 37119 is Mecklenburg County, and 37119000101 is Census Tract 1.01 in Mecklenburg County. You can read a tract GEOID from left to right like an address.
GEOIDs matter for two reasons:

Joining data. When you attach census numbers to map shapes, or combine census data with a dataset from somewhere else, the GEOID is the column you join on.
They must stay text. Many GEOIDs contain meaningful leading zeros. Alabama is 01, and the county code for Alamance County, NC is 001. If a spreadsheet program or a CSV reader turns the GEOID into a number, those zeros vanish and your joins will quietly fail. Always read GEOIDs as strings.

title: Census 101: How Census Data Is Organized
text:
Tables and variables
Census data is organized into tables, and each table holds several variables. Table IDs start with a letter that tells you what kind of table it is:








Prefix
Table type
Notes




B
Detailed table
The most granular ACS tables. These are what the code tutorials mostly use.


C
Collapsed table
A detailed table with fewer categories


S
Subject table
Summaries on one topic, often with percentages already computed


DP
Data profile
Broad overviews of social, economic, housing, and demographic traits


P, H
Decennial tables
Population (P) and housing (H) tables from the decennial census



A variable ID adds a line number to the table ID. For example, table B19013 is Median Household Income in the Past 12 Months. Its first line is B19013_001. In raw downloads and in the Census API, you will see a suffix at the end of the ID:

B19013_001E is the Estimate
B19013_001M is the Margin of error
P1_001N is a 2020 decennial count, where N stands for a number

title: Census 101: How Census Data Is Organized
text:
Downloading a table by hand
Before you write any code, it helps to find a table in the Bureau’s own tool. Let’s download median household income for every county in North Carolina.

Go to data.census.gov and click Advanced Search.
In the search box, type B19013 and press Enter. Open the table named Median Household Income in the Past 12 Months.
Click the product dropdown near the table title. Choose the most recent ACS 5-Year Estimates Detailed Tables.
Open the Geos filter. Choose County, then North Carolina, then All Counties within North Carolina.
Look over the table in your browser. Notice that each county has both an estimate and a margin of error.
Click Download Table and choose the CSV format. You will receive a ZIP file.







TipWhat’s inside the ZIP file?



The ZIP file usually holds a data file and a metadata file that describes each column. Open the data file and look at the first two rows. The first row usually contains column codes such as B19013_001E. The second row often contains longer labels. When you read the file into R or Python, keep the codes as column names and skip the label row.


Point-and-click downloads work well for one table and one geography. They become tedious when you need five tables, three years, and two kinds of geography. They are also hard to reproduce. That is why the next tutorials use code.

title: Census 101: How Census Data Is Organized
section: Other places to find census data
text:
Other places to find census data

Census Reporter is a free, friendly site for browsing ACS profiles of any place. It is great for a quick sanity check on your numbers.
IPUMS NHGIS offers historical census tables and boundary files going back to 1790. It is useful if you need to compare places over long periods.
The Census API is the service that the R and Python tutorials call behind the scenes.

title: Census 101: How Census Data Is Organized
section: Before the next tutorial: get an API key
text:
Before the next tutorial: get an API key
The Census API requires a free key for every request. Request one now at https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html. The key arrives by email within a few minutes. You have to click a link in that email to activate it.






ImportantTreat your key like a password



Don’t paste your key into a file you plan to push to GitHub. The R and Python tutorials show you how to store it safely.

title: Census 101: How Census Data Is Organized
text:
Check your understanding

You want the poverty rate for every census tract in Mecklenburg County. Which data product and which version should you use?
What does the GEOID 37119005828 refer to? Why would the GEOID 01001 cause trouble in a spreadsheet?
A friend says Cornelius has a higher median income than Huntersville, based on ACS estimates that differ by $3,000. What would you check before agreeing?







TipAnswers






The ACS 5-year estimates. Tracts don’t appear in the 1-year data, and the decennial census doesn’t ask about income.
It is Census Tract 58.28 in Mecklenburg County (37 + 119 + 005828). The GEOID 01001 (Autauga County, Alabama) would become the number 1001 in a spreadsheet. It would then fail to match the text 01001 in any other dataset.
The margins of error. If the two ranges overlap, the difference may not be meaningful.

text:
NoteAbout this tutorial



Time: about 25 minutes. Prerequisites: Census Data in Python, Part 1, including the census_helpers.py file you saved at the end of that tutorial.
By the end, you will be able to:

download county and census tract boundaries with pygris
join census data to those boundaries using the GEOID
make a choropleth map with GeoPandas and matplotlib
choose a map projection that suits North Carolina
map census tracts, remove large bodies of water, and add county outlines
make an interactive map for exploring your data

title: Census Data in Python, Part 2: Mapping with pygris and GeoPandas
text:
Why a second library?
Polars is fast and pleasant for tables. It doesn’t support geometry, though. For maps you will use GeoPandas, which adds a geometry column to a pandas DataFrame. You will download the shapes themselves with pygris. Kyle Walker wrote pygris as the Python version of tigris, the R package that tidycensus uses to fetch boundaries.
The workflow looks like this:

Pull the numbers from the Census API with get_census() from Part 1.
Pull the matching shapes with pygris.
Join the two on GEOID.
Map the result.

In R, geometry = TRUE does steps 2 and 3 for you. In Python you do them yourself, and it takes only a few more lines.

title: Census Data in Python, Part 2: Mapping with pygris and GeoPandas
text:
Setup
pip install pygris geopandas matplotlib pyarrow folium mapclassify
GeoPandas needs pyarrow to receive data from Polars. folium and mapclassify are only needed for the interactive map at the end.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import polars as pl
from matplotlib.ticker import StrMethodFormatter
from pygris import counties, tracts
from pygris.utils import erase_water

from census_helpers import get_census

A few arguments deserve a note:

cb=True requests the cartographic boundary files. These are simplified shapes that draw quickly and follow the coastline. Leave it off only if you need the precise legal boundaries.
year=2024 matches the shapes to the 2020 to 2024 ACS data you will join to them.
cache=True saves the files on your computer. The next request for the same shapes loads instantly.

The result is a GeoDataFrame with 100 rows. Its geometry column holds each county’s outline. It also has a GEOID column in the same format that get_census() produces. That shared column is what makes the join work.
Check the coordinate reference system (CRS) and make a quick plot:

print(nc_shapes.crs)
nc_shapes.plot()

EPSG:4269









The CRS is EPSG 4269, called NAD83. It stores locations as longitude and latitude.

title: Census Data in Python, Part 2: Mapping with pygris and GeoPandas
text:
Joining census data to shapes
Get median household income for each county, just as you did in Part 1:

nc_income = get_census(
    dataset="acs/acs5",
    year=2024,
    variables={
        "median_income": "B19013_001E",
        "median_income_moe": "B19013_001M",
    },
    geo_for="county:*",
    geo_in="state:37",
)

GeoPandas can’t merge with a Polars DataFrame directly, so convert it with .to_pandas() first. Keep only GEOID and geometry from the shapes. Otherwise both tables would contribute a NAME column and you would end up with NAME_x and NAME_y.

nc_map = nc_shapes[["GEOID", "geometry"]].merge(
    nc_income.to_pandas(), on="GEOID", how="left"
)

nc_map.shape

(100, 5)


Put the GeoDataFrame on the left side of the merge. The result then stays a GeoDataFrame that you can map. Using how="left" keeps every county even if its data is missing.






TipCheck your join



After any join, confirm that the rows matched. nc_map["median_income"].isna().sum() counts the counties with no data. If that number is large, compare a few GEOIDs from each table. Look for missing leading zeros, or for a GEOID that was stored as a number.

title: Census Data in Python, Part 2: Mapping with pygris and GeoPandas
text:
A choropleth map
A choropleth map shades each area by the value of a variable. GeoPandas makes one with .plot(column=...):

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 5))

nc_map.plot(
    column="median_income",
    cmap="viridis",
    edgecolor="white",
    linewidth=0.2,
    legend=True,
    legend_kwds={"orientation": "horizontal", "shrink": 0.5, "pad": 0.02},
    missing_kwds={"color": "lightgrey"},
    ax=ax,
)

ax.set_title("Median household income by county, North Carolina (2020 to 2024 ACS)")
ax.set_axis_off()
fig.axes[1].xaxis.set_major_formatter(StrMethodFormatter("${x:,.0f}"))








Here is what each piece does:

cmap="viridis" uses a color scale that is easy to read for people with color vision deficiencies.
missing_kwds draws counties with missing data in gray. Without it, those counties would disappear from the map.
ax.set_axis_off() hides the longitude and latitude ticks. They rarely help a reader.
The last line formats the legend as dollars. The legend is a second set of axes, so it lives in fig.axes[1].


Choosing a projection
Longitude and latitude describe points on a globe. Drawing them directly on a flat screen stretches the map a little. North Carolina has its own projected CRS, called NAD83 / North Carolina (EPSG 32119). Switch to it with .to_crs():

nc_map = nc_map.to_crs(32119)

Run the plotting code again and compare. The shapes will look more like official maps of the state. Projected coordinates are measured in meters, which also makes them the right choice for measuring areas and distances.

title: Census Data in Python, Part 2: Mapping with pygris and GeoPandas
text:
Mapping census tracts
The same steps work for tracts. Download Mecklenburg County’s tracts and project them:

meck_shapes = tracts(state="NC", county="Mecklenburg", cb=True, year=2024, cache=True)
meck_shapes = meck_shapes.to_crs(32119)

Using FIPS code '37' for input 'NC'
Using FIPS code '119' for input 'Mecklenburg'


pygris accepts county names, unlike the Census API. Now get the data and join:

meck_income = get_census(
    dataset="acs/acs5",
    year=2024,
    variables={
        "median_income": "B19013_001E",
        "median_income_moe": "B19013_001M",
    },
    geo_for="tract:*",
    geo_in="state:37 county:119",
)

meck_map = meck_shapes[["GEOID", "geometry"]].merge(
    meck_income.to_pandas(), on="GEOID", how="left"
)


Removing water
Census tract boundaries include water. On the northern edge of Mecklenburg County, the tracts along Lake Norman extend into the lake. erase_water() cuts large bodies of water out of your shapes:

meck_map = erase_water(meck_map, area_threshold=0.9, year=2024)

The area_threshold argument controls how much water gets erased. A value of 0.9 removes only the largest 10 percent of water features. This step can take a minute the first time you run it. You may also see a UserWarning about dropped geometries. It is safe to ignore. Now make the map:

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))

meck_map.plot(
    column="median_income",
    cmap="viridis",
    legend=True,
    legend_kwds={"shrink": 0.6},
    missing_kwds={"color": "lightgrey"},
    ax=ax,
)

ax.set_title("Median household income by census tract, Mecklenburg County")
ax.set_axis_off()
fig.axes[1].yaxis.set_major_formatter(StrMethodFormatter("${x:,.0f}"))








This legend is vertical, so the formatter goes on its yaxis.


Mapping a region with county outlines
To show tracts across several counties, download each county’s tracts and stack them. Then draw county outlines on top so readers can orient themselves. You found the FIPS codes for Iredell (097) and Cabarrus (025) in Part 1.

region_counties = ["Mecklenburg", "Iredell", "Cabarrus"]

region_shapes = tracts(
    state="NC", county=region_counties, cb=True, year=2024, cache=True
).to_crs(32119)

region_income = get_census(
    dataset="acs/acs5",
    year=2024,
    variables={"median_income": "B19013_001E"},
    geo_for="tract:*",
    geo_in="state:37 county:119,097,025",
)

region_map = region_shapes[["GEOID", "geometry"]].merge(
    region_income.to_pandas(), on="GEOID", how="left"
)

region_outlines = nc_shapes[nc_shapes["NAME"].isin(region_counties)].to_crs(32119)

Using FIPS code '37' for input 'NC'
Using FIPS code '119' for input 'Mecklenburg'
Using FIPS code '097' for input 'Iredell'
Using FIPS code '025' for input 'Cabarrus'


Plot both layers on the same axes. Use .boundary to draw the county outlines without filling them:

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))

region_map.plot(
    column="median_income",
    cmap="viridis",
    legend=True,
    legend_kwds={"shrink": 0.6},
    missing_kwds={"color": "lightgrey"},
    ax=ax,
)
region_outlines.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="white", linewidth=1)

ax.set_title("Median household income around Lake Norman")
ax.set_axis_off()
fig.axes[1].yaxis.set_major_formatter(StrMethodFormatter("${x:,.0f}"))

title: Census Data in Python, Part 2: Mapping with pygris and GeoPandas
text:
Mapping several variables at once
Small multiples put several maps side by side on one color scale. This example maps four racial and ethnic groups across Mecklenburg tracts from the 2020 Redistricting file. The data is from 2020, so use the 2020 tract shapes.

groups = {"White": "P1_003N", "Black": "P1_004N", "Asian": "P1_006N", "Hispanic": "P2_002N"}

meck_race = get_census(
    dataset="dec/pl",
    year=2020,
    variables={**groups, "total_pop": "P1_001N"},
    geo_for="tract:*",
    geo_in="state:37 county:119",
).with_columns(
    (100 * pl.col(group) / pl.col("total_pop")).alias(group) for group in groups
)

meck_race_map = (
    tracts(state="NC", county="Mecklenburg", cb=True, year=2020, cache=True)
    .to_crs(32119)[["GEOID", "geometry"]]
    .merge(meck_race.to_pandas(), on="GEOID", how="left")
)

Using FIPS code '37' for input 'NC'
Using FIPS code '119' for input 'Mecklenburg'


Loop over the groups and draw each one in its own panel. Setting vmin and vmax gives every panel the same scale, from 0 to 100 percent:

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 10))

for ax, group in zip(axes.flat, groups):
    meck_race_map.plot(
        column=group,
        cmap="magma_r",
        vmin=0,
        vmax=100,
        missing_kwds={"color": "lightgrey"},
        ax=ax,
    )
    ax.set_title(group)
    ax.set_axis_off()

fig.colorbar(
    plt.cm.ScalarMappable(norm=plt.Normalize(0, 100), cmap="magma_r"),
    ax=axes,
    shrink=0.6,
    label="Percent of tract population",
)
fig.suptitle("Race and ethnicity by census tract, Mecklenburg County (2020)")
plt.show()








The Census Bureau counts Hispanic origin separately from race. A Hispanic resident may also be counted in one of the race groups, so the four percentages can add up to more than 100.

title: Census Data in Python, Part 2: Mapping with pygris and GeoPandas
text:
Interactive maps
A static map is best for a presentation. While you explore, an interactive map lets you zoom in and hover over tracts to read their values. GeoPandas makes one with .explore():

meck_map.explore(
    column="median_income",
    cmap="viridis",
    tooltip=["NAME", "median_income", "median_income_moe"],
    tiles="Esri.WorldGrayCanvas",
)

Make this Notebook Trusted to load map: File -> Trust Notebook


The tiles argument sets the basemap. Esri’s World Gray Canvas is a light gray map with only faint roads and borders, so it doesn’t compete with your colors. It is free and needs no API key. Leave tiles out to get the default OpenStreetMap street map.
In a Jupyter notebook, the map appears below the cell. In a plain script, save it with .save("meck_income.html") and open the file in your browser.

title: Census Data in Python, Part 2: Mapping with pygris and GeoPandas
section: Attaching census shapes to other data
text:
Attaching census shapes to other data
Sometimes your data doesn’t come from the Census Bureau. It might be a table of eviction filings, school test scores, or health outcomes by tract. If it has a GEOID column, the join works exactly as it did above:

my_data = pl.read_csv("my_tract_data.csv", schema_overrides={"GEOID": pl.String})

my_map = meck_shapes[["GEOID", "geometry"]].merge(
    my_data.to_pandas(), on="GEOID", how="left"
)







WarningMatch your years



Tract boundaries changed in 2020. Data that uses 2010 tract GEOIDs won’t join cleanly to 2020 or later shapes. If many rows fail to match, check which decade’s tracts your data uses.

title: Census Data in Python, Part 2: Mapping with pygris and GeoPandas
text:
Saving maps and shapes
Save a map as an image for your slides:

fig.savefig("meck_income_map.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")

Save the spatial data itself as a GeoPackage. A GeoPackage keeps the shapes, the data, and the CRS together in one file. Teammates can open it in Python, in R, or in QGIS.

meck_map.to_file("meck_income.gpkg")







TipA shortcut for later



pygris also includes its own get_census() function in pygris.data. It sends the request and returns a pandas DataFrame, and it can build the GEOID for you. Now that you know what happens behind the scenes, feel free to use whichever version you like.

title: Census Data in Python, Part 2: Mapping with pygris and GeoPandas
text:
Try it yourself

Make a county map of the percentage of people below the poverty level in North Carolina, using the poverty data from Part 1. Project it to EPSG 32119.
Map the median gross rent (B25064_001E) for census tracts in Mecklenburg, Iredell, and Cabarrus counties. Remove the water and add county outlines. Where are rents highest?
Make a second map that shows the margin of error (B25064_001M) for the same rent data. Which areas have the least reliable estimates? How would you mention that in a presentation?

NoteAbout this tutorial



Time: about 25 minutes. Prerequisites: Census Data in R, Part 1, with your API key installed.
By the end, you will be able to:

request census data with shapes attached
make a choropleth map with ggplot2
choose a map projection that suits North Carolina
map census tracts, remove large bodies of water, and add county outlines
make an interactive map for exploring your data
attach census shapes to data from somewhere else

title: Census Data in R, Part 2: Mapping with tidycensus and sf
text:
Setup
You need three packages beyond the ones from Part 1. sf handles spatial data in R. tigris downloads Census Bureau boundary files. tidycensus uses tigris behind the scenes. leaflet makes interactive maps.

install.packages(c("sf", "tigris", "leaflet"))


library(tidycensus)
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tigris)

options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)

The tigris_use_cache option saves boundary files on your computer after the first download. That makes later requests much faster.

Adding geometry to a request

nc_income <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  state = "NC",
  variables = c(median_income = "B19013_001"),
  year = 2024,

plot(nc_income["estimate"])

title: Census Data in R, Part 2: Mapping with tidycensus and sf
text:
A choropleth map with ggplot2
A choropleth map shades each area by the value of a variable. With ggplot2, geom_sf() draws the shapes and the fill aesthetic sets the colors:

ggplot(nc_income, aes(fill = estimate)) +
  geom_sf(color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = "Median household income by county",
    subtitle = "North Carolina, 2020 to 2024 ACS 5-year estimates",
    fill = NULL,
    caption = "Source: US Census Bureau"
  ) +
  theme_void()








A few choices in that code are worth pointing out:

scale_fill_viridis_c() uses a color scale that is easy to read for people with color vision deficiencies. It also prints well in grayscale.
scales::label_dollar() formats the legend as currency.
theme_void() removes the axes and gridlines. Latitude and longitude ticks rarely help a reader.


Choosing a projection
Longitude and latitude describe points on a globe. Drawing them directly on a flat screen stretches the map. North Carolina is wide and short, so the distortion is mild, but it is still there. The state has its own projected CRS, called NAD83 / North Carolina (EPSG code 32119). You can switch to it in one line:

nc_income_proj <- st_transform(nc_income, crs = 32119)

Plot nc_income_proj with the same ggplot code and compare. The shapes will look a little more like the state you know from official maps. Projected coordinates are measured in meters. That also makes them the right choice for measuring areas and distances.

title: Census Data in R, Part 2: Mapping with tidycensus and sf
text:
Mapping census tracts
Tract maps show variation inside a county. Here is median household income for Mecklenburg County tracts:

meck_income <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "NC",
  county = "Mecklenburg",
  variables = c(median_income = "B19013_001"),
  year = 2024,
  geometry = TRUE
) |>
  st_transform(32119)

Getting data from the 2020-2024 5-year ACS

ggplot(meck_income, aes(fill = estimate)) +
  geom_sf(color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::label_dollar(), na.value = "grey80") +
  labs(
    title = "Median household income by census tract",
    subtitle = "Mecklenburg County, 2020 to 2024 ACS 5-year estimates",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_void()








Setting na.value gives tracts with suppressed estimates their own gray color. Without it, those tracts could be mistaken for part of the scale.

Removing water
Census tract boundaries include water. On the northern edge of Mecklenburg County, the tracts along Lake Norman extend into the lake. The map would look more familiar with the lake cut out. erase_water() from tigris removes large bodies of water from your shapes:

meck_income_dry <- erase_water(meck_income, area_threshold = 0.9)

Fetching area water data for your dataset's location...


Erasing water area...
If this is slow, try a larger area threshold value.


The area_threshold argument controls how much water gets erased. A value of 0.9 removes only the largest 10 percent of water features. Run the map code again with meck_income_dry to see the difference. This step can take a minute the first time you run it.


Mapping a region with county outlines
To show tracts across several counties, pass a vector of counties. Then draw county boundaries on top so readers can orient themselves:

region_counties <- c("Mecklenburg", "Iredell", "Cabarrus", "Lincoln", "Gaston")

region_income <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "NC",
  county = region_counties,
  variables = c(median_income = "B19013_001"),
  year = 2024,
  geometry = TRUE
) |>
  st_transform(32119)

Getting data from the 2020-2024 5-year ACS

region_outlines <- counties(state = "NC", cb = TRUE, year = 2024) |>
  filter(NAME %in% region_counties) |>
  st_transform(32119)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = region_income, aes(fill = estimate), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = region_outlines, fill = NA, color = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::label_dollar(), na.value = "grey80") +
  labs(title = "Median household income around Lake Norman", fill = NULL) +
  theme_void()








The cb = TRUE argument requests cartographic boundary files. These are simplified shapes that draw quickly and follow the coastline. tidycensus uses them by default when you set geometry = TRUE.

title: Census Data in R, Part 2: Mapping with tidycensus and sf
text:
Mapping several variables at once
Long-format data pairs nicely with facet_wrap(). This example maps four racial and ethnic groups across Mecklenburg tracts from the 2020 Redistricting file:

meck_race <- get_decennial(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "NC",
  county = "Mecklenburg",
  variables = c(
    White = "P1_003N",
    Black = "P1_004N",
    Asian = "P1_006N",
    Hispanic = "P2_002N"
  ),
  summary_var = "P1_001N",
  year = 2020,
  sumfile = "pl",
  geometry = TRUE
) |>
  mutate(percent = 100 * value / summary_value) |>
  st_transform(32119)

Getting data from the 2020 decennial Census


Using the PL 94-171 Redistricting Data Summary File


Note: 2020 decennial Census data use differential privacy, a technique that
introduces errors into data to preserve respondent confidentiality.
ℹ Small counts should be interpreted with caution.
ℹ See https://www.census.gov/library/fact-sheets/2021/protecting-the-confidentiality-of-the-2020-census-redistricting-data.html for additional guidance.
This message is displayed once per session.

ggplot(meck_race, aes(fill = percent)) +
  geom_sf(color = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~variable) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, na.value = "grey80") +
  labs(
    title = "Race and ethnicity by census tract, Mecklenburg County",
    subtitle = "2020 decennial census",
    fill = "Percent"
  ) +
  theme_void()








The four panels share one color scale. That makes it easy to compare where each group lives. One caution applies here. The Census Bureau counts Hispanic origin separately from race. A Hispanic resident may also be counted in one of the race groups, so the four percentages can add up to more than 100.

title: Census Data in R, Part 2: Mapping with tidycensus and sf

Interactive maps
A static map is best for a presentation. While you explore, an interactive map lets you zoom in and hover over tracts to read their values. leaflet builds interactive web maps from R. It uses the same JavaScript library that powers many of the maps you see on news sites.
leaflet expects longitude and latitude, so first transform the data to EPSG 4326 (WGS84), the standard CRS for web maps. Then build a color palette that maps each income to a color:

library(leaflet)

meck_web <- st_transform(meck_income, 4326)

income_pal <- colorNumeric("viridis", domain = meck_web$estimate)

A leaflet map is built in layers, much like a ggplot. Start with a basemap, then add the tracts, then add a legend:

leaflet(meck_web) |>
  addProviderTiles(providers$Esri.WorldGrayCanvas) |>
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~income_pal(estimate),
    fillOpacity = 0.7,
    color = "white",
    weight = 0.5,
    label = ~paste0(NAME, ": ", scales::dollar(estimate), " ± ", scales::dollar(moe))
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    pal = income_pal,
    values = ~estimate,
    title = "Median household income",
    labFormat = labelFormat(prefix = "$")
  )





Here is what each layer does:

addProviderTiles() draws a basemap underneath your data. Esri’s World Gray Canvas is a light gray map with only faint roads and borders, so it doesn’t compete with your colors. It is free and needs no API key. Some other providers, such as CARTO, now require a key. For a full street map, use addTiles() instead, which draws OpenStreetMap.
addPolygons() draws the tracts. The ~ in front of an argument tells leaflet to look up a column in your data. label sets the text that appears when you hover over a tract.
addLegend() explains the colors. It uses the same palette function as the polygons, so the two always match.

Hover over the tracts to see each estimate and its margin of error. This is a quick way to find the tracts behind a pattern you notice.

section: Attaching census shapes to other data
text:
Attaching census shapes to other data
Sometimes your data doesn’t come from the Census Bureau. It might be a table of eviction filings, school test scores, or health outcomes by tract. If the table has a GEOID column, you can download shapes with tigris and join them:

meck_tracts <- tracts(state = "NC", county = "Mecklenburg", cb = TRUE, year = 2024)

# Suppose my_data has a GEOID column stored as text
meck_joined <- meck_tracts |>
  left_join(my_data, by = "GEOID")

Put the sf object on the left side of the join. The result then stays an sf object, and ggplot2 can map it. Before you join, check that the GEOIDs in both tables are text and that they have the same number of digits.






WarningMatch your years



Tract boundaries changed in 2020. Data that uses 2010 tract GEOIDs won’t join cleanly to 2020 or later shapes. If many rows fail to match, check which decade’s tracts your data uses.

text:
Saving maps and shapes
Save a ggplot map as an image for your slides:

ggsave("meck_income_map.png", width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300)

Save the spatial data itself as a GeoPackage. A GeoPackage keeps the shapes, the data, and the CRS together in one file. Teammates can open it in R, in Python, or in QGIS.

st_write(meck_income, "meck_income.gpkg")

Map the median gross rent (B25064_001) for census tracts in Mecklenburg, Iredell, and Cabarrus counties. Remove the water and add county outlines. Where are rents highest?
